title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Irrigation servicing
audience: Irrigation servicing operators, solo or with a team, who want more work from clients that suit their registration, their area and their visit size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, visit size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that an irrigation need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the servicing jobs you can do well (seasonal checks, controller reschedules and zone reports), the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs a check. A round of seasonal checks in one suburb is worth more to a small business than a single large repair across town. List only the work that your registration and insurance cover before you start searching.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Councils buy irrigation maintenance and fault reporting on a schedule of rates: the Central Coast Council (Tasmania) tender lists it in a three-year scope (closing 10 November 2025). Strata managers have irrigation checks in their growing-season routine (Clean Group, 9 March 2026), and the committee appoints the contractor. Housing providers tender cyclical lawn and garden maintenance (CHVL tender, Victoria, closing 14 September 2025), so check whether a scope includes irrigation before you bid. Record each contact's source and date, use only business contact details published for business use, and do not buy lists (ACMA, Spam Act obligations, last updated 28 March 2019). Confirm scope, capacity and deadline before quoting (Business Queensland, 16 November 2022).

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: Public tenders are the clearest signal. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (Buying for Victoria, 7 August 2026). Other states run their own portals, and national tender listings show councils in other states. Planning permit registers show projects at application stage. The Victorian building permit dataset records each permit's location, estimated cost and issue date, and can be filtered by suburb or postcode, but the page read does not show owner or builder names (DataVic, updated 28 August 2026). Use such data for area-level planning, not for individual contact with a home.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A first message names how you learned of the need, makes one verifiable observation (for example, a tender scope that includes fault reporting you can meet), and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area. Keep it short and make it easy to say no. Check the consent and unsubscribe rules before any email or text (ACMA). The ACCC's July 2026 review found that many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the number and timing of follow-ups before the first message. Remove a prospect at once when asked to stop, and record the request and its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the servicing criteria for service area, visit size, repeat need and registration held.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as tender alerts, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the registration rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A Victorian technician sees a Tasmanian council tender for irrigation maintenance and fault reporting in a national tender listing. The technician works only in Victoria and is not sure whether the Victorian registration covers the servicing in the tender.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the technician respond to the council tender, and what should the first step be?
workedExamples.reasoning: A tender in another state is outside the technician's own market, and the business should bid only where its registration, insurance and local rules allow. The first step is to check the tender's own portal and eligibility rules for that state, and to confirm whether the registration covers the work before any bid. If the technician wants to email a named council officer, the Spam Act applies: publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages (ACMA). The technician does not contact residents or property owners about their systems using personal details.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, visit size, repeat need and registration held
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a repair you are not registered or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the registration and insurance before outreach, and remove that work from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a registered or licensed service in outreach unless you hold the registration or licence that the state where the work is done requires. In Victoria, the VBA lists non-agricultural irrigation as a registered plumbing class, and this lesson does not say whether servicing needs it. NSW irrigation licensing is not confirmed. This lesson does not grant any registration or licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. ACMA's avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is not confirmed in this lesson.

Telemarketing calls to registered numbers are limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and never on Sundays or public holidays (Do Not Call Register industry guide, 2018 copyright notice; check for updates). Wash any call list against the register before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the servicing work you want, within your registration, before you filter prospects.
Watch public signals, such as tenders, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public tender for irrigation maintenance is listed in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Respond through the tender's own route, after checking that you can meet its scope, schedule and registration rules
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the work
Go onto the site to look at the system and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Says marketing messages need consent, which must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and carry correct contact details; every commercial message needs a free unsubscribe option honoured within five working days. Publisher: ACMA.
